title: Looking Back to Leap Ahead
question: What was reborn in the Renaissance, and where did it start?
hook: A movement that dug up the ancient past helped change how Europe made art, wrote about politics and handled money.
idea: The Renaissance revived the achievements of classical antiquity, starting in Florence and spreading across Europe.

beats.prompt: A scholar in the 1400s wants fresh ideas about art, thought and politics. Where would a Renaissance humanist most likely look?

choices.label: Back to the writings and art of ancient Greece and Rome
Only to brand-new inventions with no link to the past
choices.feedback: Inventions mattered, but the movement was characterized by reviving ancient achievements.

choices.label: To the medieval Arabic works on natural science alone
choices.feedback: That was the focus of earlier 12th-century scholars, not what set the Renaissance apart.

beats.explain: The Renaissance was characterized by the rediscovery and revival of the literary, philosophical and artistic achievements of classical antiquity.

beats.prompt: Put these Renaissance moments in order.
items: First traces appear in Italy with Dante and Giotto
A resurgence of learning based on classical sources
Pico della Mirandola writes the Oration on the Dignity of Man
Charles V's assault on Rome ends the Italian Renaissance
beats.explain: Traces began in the late 13th century, the learning revival came in the 14th, Pico wrote in 1486, and the Italian Renaissance concluded in 1527.

beats.prompt: Match each thinker or artist to what they are tied to.
pairs: Credited with the 14th-century resurgence of learning
Led painters striving to portray the human form realistically
Sought to describe political life as it really was
Wrote the Oration on the Dignity of Man
beats.explain: Each worked in a different field, from learning to painting to politics to philosophy, but all belong to the same movement.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: The Renaissance began in Florence and spread through Italy and Europe.
Its scholars revived literary and artistic achievements of antiquity.
So Renaissance humanists rejected Christianity, and the Church had no part in its art.
Yet many of the Renaissance's greatest works were devoted to Christianity.
beats.explain: Humanists did not reject Christianity, and the Church patronized many works of Renaissance art.
